The timeline, layout, colour grammar and nameplate are core and stay in responsibility-laundering.js. Schema: CONVENTIONS.md, Editions; figure-specific keys: draft (the AI's draft, as SVG lines, and the phrase the first person's answer leans on), note, questions, answers. page.checkFollow and page.quotes use [text](href) links and *em*, filled by the figure (data-rl-rich).

task.label: EXAMPLE TASK
task.text: Recommend when to evacuate a port city.

questions: 1 · Suppose the port closes. Who made this call?
2 · Why did you rely on it?

first: “I signed it. The analysis said ships could do it.”
“It was the AI’s estimate. It seemed solid.”
second: “I did. I chose to rely on the estimate.”
“It assumes an open port. Today’s reports looked normal, so I accepted it. I should have checked for closures.”

beats.detail: a task card appears at the top left: "Example task: Recommend when to evacuate a port city." Two red dots appear, labelled {first} and {second}.

beats.text: Suppose the same prompt gives both the same AI draft.
beats.detail: both dots pulse. A sheet fills at the centre in grey on a beige band: "The analysis estimates ships can carry everyone out." "It is recommended that civilians wait for ships." It divides into two identical copies, labelled "{first}'s copy, drafted with AI" and "{second}'s copy, drafted with AI".

beats.text: Both {people} read it closely and agree.
beats.detail: a key below names the beige band "Written by AI". Both dots read along every line of their copies, at the same pace and at the same time. Nothing changes.

beats.text: The first {person} signs. The second notes what the estimate rests on, then signs.
beats.detail: the first dot signs in red, and the key adds "{A_person}'s decision" in red. The second dot moves above its copy, into a row labelled "Their own note, not handed in", and writes a red note: "Rests on an open port. Today's harbor reports: normal." The first {person}'s cell shows a dash. Then the second dot signs. The note stays.

the note row dims under "{reviewer_doesnt_see}", and a frame labelled "{what_reviewer_sees}" goes round the two copies. "1. Suppose the port closes. Who made this call?" The first {person} says, "I signed it. The analysis said ships could do it." The second says, "I did. I chose to rely on the estimate."

"2. Why did you rely on it?" The first {person} says, "It was the AI's estimate. It seemed solid." The second says, "It assumes an open port. Today's reports looked normal, so I accepted it. I should have checked for closures."

beats.text: The first gives the AI's reason. The second gives their own.
beats.detail: the frame goes and the note returns. "The analysis" is outlined in the first {person}'s answer and on their copy. The first {person}'s dot halves: one half stays at the signature, and the other moves beside "The analysis estimates" and becomes a hollow dashed grey ring, keyed "Reason handed to the AI". It stays. A red bracket marks the second {person}'s second answer, their own reason; their dot stays whole.

beats.text: Suppose it proves wrong. The AI can't answer for it. Both {people} will.
beats.detail: a navy weight labelled "Answerable" falls down the first paper's margin, past the AI's sentences and the grey ring, and rests on the first {person}'s half dot at the signature. A second weight falls down the second paper's margin and rests on the second {person}.

page.title: Responsibility laundering
page.description: A teaching figure: two {people} sign the same AI-drafted recommendation, and faculty find out who can account for it by asking why they relied on the AI's estimate.
page.setup: Suppose two {people} give an AI the same prompt, get the same draft, and sign it as written. *The Irreducible Officer* calls the risk responsibility laundering: a recommendation becomes easier to defend because the model generated it, or easier to soften because the model's language distributes agency. The figure runs about a minute and a half. The task, the draft and both {people} are a constructed example.
page.srTitle: Responsibility laundering, an animated figure in nine beats after its name card
page.srSummary: An animated figure, "Responsibility laundering", failure mode 7 of 7. It opens on its name, which then stays in the top-left corner. Two red dots stand for two {people} with an example task: recommend when to evacuate a port city. Suppose the same prompt gives both the same AI draft, shown in grey, the figure's mark for words the AI wrote: "The analysis estimates ships can carry everyone out. It is recommended that civilians wait for ships." The draft divides into two copies, one for each {person}, both marked "drafted with AI". Both {people} read it closely, at the same pace, and agree. The first signs in red. The second first writes a red note in a row labelled "their own note, not handed in": "Rests on an open port. Today's harbor reports: normal." Then they sign. While {reviewer_ask_l}, the note row dims under "{reviewer_doesnt_see}", and a frame labelled "{what_reviewer_sees}" goes round the two identical copies. {reviewer_asks_each}: "Suppose the port closes. Who made this call?" The first says, "I signed it. The analysis said ships could do it." The second says, "I did. I chose to rely on the estimate." Then: "Why did you rely on it?" The first says, "It was the AI's estimate. It seemed solid." The second says, "It assumes an open port. Today's reports looked normal, so I accepted it. I should have checked for closures." Then the note returns. "The analysis" is outlined in the first {person}'s answer and on their copy, and the first {person}'s dot halves: one half stays at the signature, and the other moves beside "The analysis estimates" and becomes a hollow dashed grey ring, keyed "reason handed to the AI", where it stays. A red bracket marks the second {person}'s answer, their own reason; their dot stays whole. Two navy weights labelled "Answerable" fall, one down each paper's margin, past the AI's sentences, and rest on each {person}'s dot at the signature. The figure ends on the name and its definition, "The model’s recommendation makes agency feel shared, or easier to defend.", above the {check_l}. Each beat is listed below with what is on screen.
checkLines: Who owns the recommendation if it proves wrong?
Name one way it could prove wrong. Ask why they relied on it.
page.checkFollow: Both {people} signed the same paper. If it proves wrong, both answer for it, and the AI can't. Asked who owns it, both would say they do. Asked why they relied on the AI's estimate, the first {person} says it seemed solid. The second says what the estimate assumed, why they accepted that, and the check they should have made. Both answer for the call. Only the second can say what it rested on. That answer is hard to give without having asked the question before signing, and the second {person}'s note shows they did. Section VII of the essay asks students to say why they accepted an output, why they rejected one, and why they remain accountable for the recommendation despite the system's contribution. The companion's [failure-mode lab](https://judgmentlab.net/#companion) makes a related point about a signed statement of responsibility: it can add evidence, but it doesn't show that the learner can defend the judgment. The lab also notes the cost: with many learners, faculty have to sample rather than question everyone. Whether relying on the estimate was justified is a separate check, covered by [uncalibrated reliance](../uncalibrated-reliance/).

paras: Responsibility laundering is the final danger. A recommendation becomes easier to defend because the model generated it, or easier to soften because the model's language distributes agency. The analysis lands with the apparent weight of objectivity. But AI does not become accountable for the recommendation. The human remains responsible for the final judgment. When the recommendation proves wrong, shaped by assumptions no one examined and optimizing toward a target no one explicitly chose, the question of who chose the frame does not have a satisfying answer.
quotes.cite: *The Irreducible Officer*, Section II, What the Problem Looks Like

paras: … A human recommendation brings context with it. Experience, incentives, reputation, and the way a person answers when pressed all travel with the recommendation. A commander can weigh those signals. A model carries none of them and can still sound equally confident. It can support a judgment, but it cannot provide the human presence that makes accountability clear to subordinates, partners, or commanders who will live with the result.

First-person ownership matters in the classroom. The student should be able to say why they accepted an output, why they rejected one, and why they remain accountable for the recommendation despite the system's contribution. Students are practicing the accountability structure their professional roles will require.
